- No render refusals or waits; the longest queue was 35.7 s for the route run. No reference image was blocked.. Judge: B was clearly better in all four pairs, and none was close. The B frames read as marketing-grade AAA captures, and two of them carry a title watermark. I judged them only on what is visible. They win on four points: a dense, believable world all the way to the horizon; directional sunlight with real atmospheric perspective (backlit glitter, haze layering, lens flare); rich, varied materials; and a hero subject with dynamic simulation (turbulent foam wakes, crashing spray, rotor blur). All four A frames come from the same harbour city and share the same failures. The city art is still at blockout level: extruded towers with one tiled facade, cloned dome-topped blocks, identical evenly spaced trees, untextured beige boxes, towers on white plinths, flat empty landmasses and container ships floating in fog. The lighting is a flat lavender overcast with no clear sun, no rim light and only shallow haze, so the sunlit and backlit settings the contexts describe never appear. Life is sparse: few boats, no visible people, empty roads. The water simulation is stylized: wakes are thin straight streaks, whitecaps are uniform noise even in a sheltered harbour, and quay foam is a constant white line. The strengths of A are the near-field water shading (normal detail, long tower reflections, sun sparkle), a recognisable landmark layout, a clean HUD, and a decent Ferris wheel. To compete, the priorities in order are: populate and detail the environment out to the horizon and remove placeholder geometry; establish a real sun with atmospheric depth; replace the streak wakes and noise whitecaps with foam that responds to boats and structures; and give hero vehicles motion blur and spray. None of the A frames wows. Three of the four B frames do (lighthouse, helicopter, train); the speedboat promo is strong but more ordinary.
